gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1013r:
Managerial Cost Accounting Practices, GAO-05-1013R of September 2, 2005, asks how well federal agencies count what their work costs. Laws such as the Chief Financial Officers Act of 1990 and the Federal Financial Management Improvement Act of 1996 push agencies to build sound cost data. Good cost data ties staff time and cash to goals, plans, and results.

GAO asked how agencies build such data and how chiefs use it to steer work. Case work at the Labor and Veterans Affairs departments anchors the study. The verdict in the title is blunt: strong chiefs and tight checks on the books are the keys to making cost counts work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1033r:
A twin audit letter, GAO-05-1033R of September 30, 2005, covers the National Conference of State Societies, Washington, District of Columbia. Like its twin, the group holds a federal charter. Such groups must send Congress a yearly audit of their books. GAO reads each audit and tells Congress if the books raise flags.

GAO checked the audit reports for fiscal years 2003 and 2002. The auditors said the books were fairly shown on a cash basis of accounting. GAO found no case of rule-breaking worth a report. The letter is brief: scope, the auditors' clean view, and GAO's own no-flags result.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-503r:
Former Members of Congress, Incorporated, has its audit report reviewed in GAO-05-503R, a GAO letter dated June 10, 2005. The group works to deepen public grasp of Congress as an institution. It also promotes understanding of representative democracy, at home and abroad. The single year under review ended December 31, 2003.

Yearly audited statements are a legal duty for corporations that hold a federal charter. The statements must show assets and liabilities and give fair detail on income and expenses. GAO read this group's statements, notes, and audit report. It applied analytical checks to the figures shown. Nothing in the papers broke the reporting rules of the statute. The outside auditor's opinion was that the statements were fairly presented under standard U.S. accounting rules. GAO is clear that it rendered no opinion of its own and did not audit the group.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-513r:
Congressional Medal of Honor Society business fills GAO letter GAO-05-513R, sent June 10, 2005. The society guards the dignity and honor of the Medal itself. It shields recipients from exploitation, fosters patriotism, and urges youth toward worthy citizenship. The audit report under review covers the fiscal year ended December 31, 2003.

Like other chartered corporations, the society must file yearly financial statements with fair detail on income and expenses. An independent public accountant must audit those statements. GAO read the statements and the auditor's report and checked the figures with simple analysis. Its objective was to report any matter of noncompliance to Congress. It identified none. The auditor held the statements fairly presented in accordance with United States generally accepted accounting principles. GAO notes it is not rendering an audit opinion.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-553r:
Internal controls at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation are the subject of a GAO management letter, GAO-05-553R, dated June 10, 2005. In February 2005 GAO gave its opinions on the 2004 statements of the three funds the corporation runs. This letter covers smaller faults found during those audits. None was large enough to change the statements. GAO still judged that each one deserved management attention and a fix.

Three faults stand out. The corporation made errors in the math behind its allowance for losses on thrift resolution claims. Those errors would have misstated two of the funds. Controls were also weak over pay figures tied to the Thrift Savings Plan. Mistakes there could have flowed into the funds' books. A third fault let contractor billing errors pass unseen. The corporation overpaid as a result.  GAO made three recommendations to tighten the procedures.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-593r:
The Labor Department's representation letter for fiscal year 2004 is assessed in GAO letter GAO-05-593R, dated June 23, 2005. Written representations from agency leaders are a required part of the audit of the government's combined financial statements. GAO scored the letter across five key areas. Three areas needed improvement, though the gaps were limited in scale.

The department omitted its materiality thresholds, the measures of what counts as a material matter in its books. Its letter nonetheless held 28 of the 29 standard representations that applied, the strongest showing in this group. The single remaining item was included only in part. A third fault lay in the error summary. The list of uncorrected misstatements was incomplete, and it mixed errors in accounts with other agencies together with errors in public accounts. GAO directed three recommendations to the chief financial officer. The inspector general was asked to assist with future letters.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-603r:
In GAO-05-603R (July 22, 2005), GAO turns to the Environmental Protection Agency's representation letter for fiscal year 2004. The letter underwrites the audit of the government's consolidated financial statements. GAO measured it against five key areas from the audit manual. Two areas fell short, both in the letter's supporting detail rather than its main confirmations.

The letter held 28 of the 29 standard representations that applied to the agency. The other one was included only in part. The summary of uncorrected misstatements was incomplete. It gave no description of the errors, and it did not split errors in accounts with other agencies from errors in accounts with the public. GAO made two recommendations to the chief financial officer. It asked the inspector general to work with the agency on future letters. The finance office replied that it has taken, or will take, action on the recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-693r:
Smaller flaws in the securities agency's bookkeeping get their own list in GAO-05-693R, a management report dated August 12, 2005. It grows out of GAO's audit of the agency's fiscal 2004 statements. That audit found three material weaknesses, handled in two companion reports. This letter covers the rest: faults too small to sway the statements but worth fixing anyway. Each item comes with a recommendation.

Together the three reports map the audit's full advice, from material weakness down to housekeeping. The aim is tighter day-to-day accounting before small slips grow into audit findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-733r: GAO letter GAO-05-733R, dated July 14, 2005, gives the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services data on what hospitals paid for radiopharmaceuticals. Medicare pays set rates for outpatient care, and new drugs raised fears that rates lagged real costs. The law directed GAO to survey a large sample of hospitals. The hosted text keeps the letter's opening and its rate-setting context, so readers can see why the price data was gathered for CMS.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-893r:
More written answers on Amtrak's dining service appear in GAO-05-893R, a letter dated July 11, 2005. GAO had testified on June 9, 2005, to a House railroads panel. The hearing covered Amtrak food and beverage operations. Lawmakers sent follow-up questions after the hearing. This letter answers them for the record.

The answers extend GAO's audit of how Amtrak runs food and drink on its trains. They add detail on the contract, costs, and controls behind the testimony. Readers who want the full record can pair the letter with the hearing account. The letter stands as the formal follow-up Congress asked for.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-933r:
High energy laser planning at the Defense Department is reviewed in GAO-05-933R, a letter from July 28, 2005. A 2000 master plan set up a joint office to revive laser technology. Congress told the department to report on that office's results. GAO judged the department's assessment. It asked whether the assessment meets congressional concerns.

GAO found the assessment generally responsive. The joint office has largely met the goals set in a 2001 law, GAO agreed. Funding growth shows commitment, the department argued. But the report lacks detail on how and when laser technology will reach the warfighter. A draft energy roadmap may supply that detail. It is not yet official policy. Funding duty for the office has also shifted from the defense secretary's office to the Air Force, the letter notes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1053r:
A restatement database update is sent in GAO-06-1053R, a letter dated August 31, 2006. On July 24, 2006, GAO reported on public company restatements to Congress. That report listed 1,390 announcements made for fraud or accounting errors. The window ran from July 1, 2002, to September 30, 2005. Congress asked for a limited update of the same database.

The update covers October 1, 2005, through June 30, 2006. It extends the listing of restatement announcements on the same terms as the July report. Readers tracking market and enforcement trends get the added months in matching form. The letter is a data transmittal, short by design. It keeps the series continuous for the committees that ordered the work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-243r:
Buying steroids without a prescription proves easy in GAO-06-243R, a letter report dated November 3, 2005. Congress asked GAO to test whether illegal anabolic steroids can be bought with no doctor's note. It asked whether such buys are simple to make. It also asked where illegal steroids commonly come from. And it asked what makes the trade hard for police to fight. GAO ran test purchases and spoke with law enforcement staff for this study.

The title states the result in plain terms. Steroids are easily purchased without a prescription. Sellers ship from abroad and through online channels that shift fast. Police face hard proof problems in tracing supply chains. Cases are small, spread out, and low on agency priority lists. The letter gives Congress a ground-level test, not just claims about the trade. It shows how a banned drug stays within easy reach of any buyer with a mailbox.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-323r:
Written answers on the security clearance backlog make up GAO-06-323R, a letter dated January 17, 2006. On November 9, 2005, GAO testified at a Senate hearing on fixing the clearance process. The hearing was the second part of a series on delayed access. Afterward, Senator Akaka sent three questions for the record. This letter answers them. The questions concern the defense department's own clearance program. They also concern the government's wider plan to speed and improve clearances across agencies.

Clearances gate who may hold sensitive jobs and contracts. Slow or uneven vetting stalls hiring and raises costs. The exchange shows oversight at its most granular: a senator's written questions, an agency's written replies. Such letters rarely make news. They build the record on which reform bills rest. Readers tracking the clearance debate will find commitments stated here in black and white.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-373r:
Federal block grant money can drift when state use goes unchecked. A GAO letter, GAO-06-373R of February 7, 2006, reviews the Community Services Block Grant program. A House committee asked GAO to study the program. The Department of Health and Human Services runs it. Its Office of Community Services holds the main duty for the grants.

GAO focused on how the department monitors states that get grant funds. That narrow focus is the heart of the letter. The title gives GAO's conclusion. The department needs to improve its monitoring of state grantees. Readers learn why oversight of state spending matters. They also see the office charged with that work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-443r:
Moving sick patients out of a storm's path is among the hardest rescue tasks. A GAO letter report, GAO-06-443R of February 16, 2006, gives early observations on evacuating hospitals and nursing homes. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita drove the review. Federal officials used the National Disaster Medical System to move Katrina patients. That was the system's first use for so many patients.

GAO asked who decides to evacuate such facilities. It studied what issues managers weigh in that choice. It also mapped federal help for such moves. A Senate panel asked for the briefing that this letter records. Readers see decision points for fragile patients.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-463r:
Saving a species takes time and money, yet plans rarely say how much of either. A GAO letter, GAO-06-463R of April 6, 2006, studies recovery plans under the Endangered Species Act of 1973. About 1,300 domestic species have been listed as threatened or endangered. Only 9 have gone extinct and 17 have recovered, the letter notes. Two agencies write recovery plans for listed species.

GAO sampled 107 recovery plans. It checked whether they state total time and cost to recover a species. It also checked for three key elements from a 1988 amendment. Time and costs are largely unknown, GAO found. Readers get plan-level evidence for a long debate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-503r:
Scholars in the humanities keep a chartered council, and its audit passes review. Letter GAO-06-503R, dated March 14, 2006, covers the American Council of Learned Societies. The audit reports run for the years ended September 30, 2003, and 2002. The council works to advance studies in all fields of learning. It also works to strengthen ties among the national groups devoted to such studies in each field.

By law, such chartered groups must present their assets, debts, income, and costs in yearly statements. An outside public accountant must audit those statements. GAO read the statements and the reports of the auditor. It found no reportable case of failure to follow the law. The auditor said the statements were presented fairly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-543r:
The tax agency's own internal controls are detailed in this management report. Letter GAO-06-543R, dated May 12, 2006, follows GAO's audit of the Internal Revenue Service. In November 2005, GAO reported on the agency's statements for fiscal years ended September 30, 2005 and 2004. It also reported on controls as of September 30, 2005. Compliance with selected laws was covered as well.

This report discusses control issues found in that audit. They are issues that could be improved. For these, GAO has no recommendations currently outstanding. All of them warrant management attention, GAO says. A separate report on past recommendations was to follow shortly. Readers get the detailed findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-663r:
Security grants for nonprofit groups are covered in GAO-06-663R, a letter report GAO issued on May 22, 2006. The fiscal year 2005 homeland security appropriation set aside $25 million for nonprofits at high risk of a terrorist attack. The money came out of $885 million for the Urban Areas Security Initiative. The Department of Homeland Security had to decide which groups qualified as high risk.

Rather than pick the groups itself, the department delegated selection to selected states. GAO found that states used a variety of approaches to judge risk and choose award winners. Those differences meant similar groups could face different tests depending on their state. The report records an early try at moving counterterrorism aid beyond government agencies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-683r:
A veterans group's audit is reviewed in GAO-06-683R, a short GAO letter report dated May 12, 2006. The Legion of Valor of the United States of America holds a federal charter. Its members earned the nation's top medals for valor in combat. The group's purposes include honoring the actions behind those medals and advancing the interests of service members. Federal law requires such chartered groups to publish yearly financial statements and obtain an outside audit.

GAO reviewed the audit reports for the fiscal year ended April 30, 2003. GAO found no reportable instances of noncompliance with the law's financial reporting rules. The outside auditor had judged that the statements were fairly presented. GAO's letter passes that result to Congress, which keeps oversight of chartered corporations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-783r:
Fast-track buying powers at the Homeland Security Department are reported in GAO-06-783R, a letter dated June 20, 2006. When Congress created the department after September 11, 2001, some feared it could not buy fast enough in an emergency. Section 833 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 granted special streamlined acquisition authorities. These powers relax some normal procurement rules to speed urgent buys. GAO reported on how the department had used them.

The letter records the department's use of the special authorities since they were granted. It places that use against the emergency aims Congress had in mind. Such powers trade normal safeguards for speed, so their record matters. Readers can see whether a rare tool stayed rare. The report supports oversight of emergency procurement as the department matured.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-853r:
Follow-up answers on the FBI's Trilogy project fill GAO-06-853R, a letter report dated June 9, 2006. The letter answers a congressional request tied to a hearing of May 2, 2006, titled FBI Oversight. It draws largely on GAO's published report on Trilogy, numbered GAO-06-306. That report found weak controls over contractor payments and missing gear. Members wanted more detail on the findings and on what they mean for the bureau's next system, Sentinel.

GAO warned that the same flaws could haunt future projects. Without firm controls over contractor payments and purchased equipment, new efforts would be highly vulnerable. The letter restates the core lessons of the Trilogy case in answer form. It shows how an oversight hearing extends the life of an audit. Readers get the pointed questions and GAO's replies in one record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-913r:
U.S. military basing plans abroad are tracked in GAO letter GAO-06-913R, dated August 22, 2006. In 2004 the President set out the widest reshaping of U.S. forces overseas since the Korean War. New bases and sites would cost billions, split between the United States and host nations.

The Senate had told the Defense Department to write full master plans for each overseas command. GAO judged the plans sent to Congress on April 27, 2006. It checked them against the Senate's stated needs, and checked the guidance behind them. The letter is one yearly check in a long watch over global basing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-923r:
Big Brothers-Big Sisters of America is the chartered group behind GAO letter GAO-06-923R, dated July 7, 2006. The group's stated aim is to help people across the country meet social and money problems, and to grow in health, learning, and character. Federal charter law calls for an outside audit each year.

GAO read the audit report for the fiscal year that ended March 31, 2004. In the auditor's view, the statements were fairly shown under U.S. accounting rules. GAO found no breach that had to be reported. The letter records that result for Congress, as part of the standing audit watch over chartered groups.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1013r:
A makeover at the immigration services agency is reviewed in GAO letter GAO-07-1013R, dated July 17, 2007. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services had spent 4 years on scattered, unplanned updates. In 2006 it folded that work into a wide revamp of its process and tech.

The revamp aims at security, service, and speed. It runs to 2013, at a cost of up to $536 million, paid mostly from fees. Law held back $47 million until GAO reviewed the plans. GAO checked the May 2007 plans against proven revamp steps, and for facts Congress asked for. Gains in performance, staffing, and tech care are needed, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1143r:
Trial housing after disaster gives lessons for future contests, GAO reports in letter GAO-07-1143R, dated August 31, 2007. The emergency agency houses victims in trailers and factory-built homes for up to 18 months. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005 wrecked Gulf Coast homes and left thousands in need for far longer.

Congress gave $400 million for pilot housing plans in the five Gulf states. In December 2006 awards went to Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, and Alabama, led by up to $281.3 million for Mississippi. GAO checked how bids were sought, scored, and priced. It set that path beside like grant contests at other agencies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1203r:
Fort Monmouth in New Jersey was set to close under the 2005 round of base closures. Dated September 6, 2007, GAO-07-1203R is a letter that follows up on that round. It sums up GAO's public observations on the 2005 Base Realignment and Closure process. It also reviews the method behind a coming Defense Department report. That report covers moving technical work from Fort Monmouth to Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland.

GAO had found the Pentagon's overall process for picking bases to be sound. The choices were generally logical, well documented, and reasoned. But GAO flagged limits in the cost and savings estimates behind them. Some savings may have been overstated, it warned. GAO also raised concern about losing skilled staff who would not move.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1233r:
A tape company official claimed that agencies sell used data tapes holding sensitive records. Congress asked GAO to test the risk, and GAO answered in GAO-07-1233R on September 21, 2007. Federal rules do not require erasing all data from all tapes before disposal. National standards do call for cleaning tapes that hold certain sensitive data. GAO bought used tapes from the one reseller it found that buys from the government.

GAO could find no readable data on the tapes it tested. The reseller said it erases most tapes by degaussing before resale. That process wipes data fully and blocks recovery. One catch involves tapes with servo tracks, which degaussing would destroy. For those, the firm used a different cleaning method. GAO's title gives its bottom line: the sale presents a low security risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-23r:
A land program from 1887 still takes applications, though almost no land remains for it. GAO called the program dead in GAO-07-23R, a letter dated October 20, 2006. The General Allotment Act let individual Indians claim parcels of public land. Later laws withdrew nearly all public land from such claims. The land bureau still holds the authority to issue allotments. GAO judged whether the program can still work.

Of 22 applications GAO reviewed, the bureau denied 18 and approved 2. Two more were withdrawn by the applicants. The only approvals in 20 years were two in Arizona in 1990. The bureau still gets one to five applications a year. Land left for disposal cannot support a family, as the program requires. Issuing allotments also fights the push to join split Indian land holdings. GAO urged a repeal proposal, and the Interior Department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-243r:
Since 1992, the United States has judged its nuclear arsenal without exploding a single test device. GAO described the yearly check behind that judgment in GAO-07-243R, dated February 2, 2007. A 2003 law requires the annual assessment. The directors of three weapons labs write reports on each weapon type. The head of Strategic Command adds a view on military effect. The Energy and Defense secretaries must pass the reports to the President unchanged.

The letters are due to the President by March 1 each year. He must send them to Congress by March 15. A joint Nuclear Weapons Council helps the secretaries frame their conclusions. That council also advises if any problem might force a return to testing. GAO traced the 2005 and 2006 cycles for this letter. It spoke with lab staff, command staff, and the reports' end users. The letter maps each step and each sign-off.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-263r:
An obscure agency guards federal workers who report wrongdoing, and its case handling drew questions. GAO described its procedures in GAO-07-263R, a letter dated January 12, 2007. The Office of Special Counsel takes complaints about banned personnel acts. It also runs a safe channel for disclosures. Two cases under the Hatch Act had raised fairness concerns in the press. GAO mapped how cases get assigned.

Most paper flows through a document control branch first, GAO found. Staff sort items and open case files there. Four units then handle complaints, disclosures, Hatch Act matters, and veterans' cases. The agency head may assign any case personally. In practice, career unit chiefs make most assignments. They weigh the claim type, staff skill, and workload. Cases outside the agency's reach close with a letter. In fiscal year 2005 the agency took 1,771 personnel complaints and 485 disclosures.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-323r: GAO reviews outside audits for groups that hold federal charters. This letter, GAO-07-323R of January 26, 2007, covers the Navy Club of the United States of America. The audit checked the club's books for fiscal year 2005. The outside auditors held that the statements were presented fairly, in line with standard accounting rules. GAO checked their work. It found no breaches of law or rule worth reporting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-333r:
New high-security labs for germ research are rising across the country with federal construction money. GAO answered Congress's questions about them in GAO-07-333R, dated February 22, 2007. The allergy and infectious disease institute funds two lab programs. One builds national labs up to the highest safety level. The other builds regional labs one tier lower. Grants went out in fiscal years 2003 and 2005. As of January 2007, none of the labs was running.

The letter responds to a request sent November 30, 2005. It covers design rules and safety guidance for the labs. It lists factors used in awarding construction funds. It describes how the institute talks with the public about sites. It also outlines the labs' research agendas. Enclosures list agents that could serve as bioweapons. They give sample rules for lab operations and security. The labs exist because the 2001 anthrax attacks exposed weak readiness.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-33r:
A fraud hotline tip led GAO to a $354 million embassy security contract awarded without competition. This letter, GAO-07-33R of November 8, 2006, reports the small-business side of the case. The State Department hired a joint venture in March 2003. The venture pairs a large mentor firm with a small protégé firm. The pairing sits in a federal program for disadvantaged businesses. GAO asked why no rivals bid. It also asked whether the small business agency watched the venture.

The award rested on an improper waiver, GAO found. In 2001 the agency had waived competition limits in blanket form. Its rules allow waivers only for named buys. Headquarters staff did not know the waiver existed until GAO raised it. Oversight of the venture was also absent. The mentor and a subcontractor do the security installs. The protégé mostly runs a warehouse and paperwork. The agency agreed to retract the waiver.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-363r:
Congress asked a precise question about the $20 million in duplicate hurricane payments: improper, or potentially improper? GAO answered in GAO-07-363R, a letter dated January 12, 2007. The question followed GAO's December 6, 2006 testimony on relief fraud. The relief agency paid some victims for the same damage under both storms. GAO explains how the $20 million figure was built. It also states what case-level probing found.

The $20 million is a potential figure, GAO replied. It came from data mining, not case-by-case proof. GAO did probe 12 registrations from 6 people. All 6 had drawn duplicate payments for one home. In one case, the same person got two payments of $10,500 to replace the same house. The estimate is likely low, GAO added. It counts only matches on the same Social Security number and address.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-423r:
The tax gap for tax year 2001 reached $345 billion, and GAO-07-423R, issued March 15, 2007, shows how audit data could shrink it. The gap is the sum owed under law minus what filers pay on time. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) gauged it through its National Research Program, a close review of about 46,000 returns. It was the first such study since tax year 1988.

GAO mined the study data for weak spots worth more research. Each 1 percent cut in the net gap would yield about $3 billion a year. One flaw stood out: IRS could not always find or reach its exam case files. GAO told IRS to plan a full electronic capture of those files. The IRS chief agreed with the step.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-443r:
U.S. aid to the West Bank and Gaza is tracked in GAO-07-443R, released March 5, 2007. Since fiscal year 1993, the United States had sent more than $2.2 billion to back the peace process. In fiscal years 2005 and 2006 alone, over $420 million in Economic Support Funds flowed in. The U.S. Agency for International Development ran most of the aid. In January 2006, Hamas won a majority in the Palestinian parliament.

Congress told GAO to check how the funds were used. GAO traced pledges and spending for both years. It took a closer look at the 2005 extra funding round. The test was whether the agency split funds as Congress directed, across growth and building categories. The report gives lawmakers a ledger for a fraught aid stream.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-473r:
Military chaplains have a chartered support group, and GAO-07-473R, dated March 9, 2007, reviews its audit. The Military Chaplains Association of the United States of America helps chaplains do their duties well. It also works to draw new people into the chaplaincy. As a federally chartered corporation, it must file yearly financial statements and get an outside audit under 36 U.S.C. 10101.

The letter covers the fiscal years ended December 31, 2004 and 2003. GAO read the audit reports and the statements and notes behind them. It ran checks on the numbers but did not audit the group itself. No instance of noncompliance was found that needed reporting. The auditors' opinions said the statements were fairly presented under standard accounting rules. GAO sent the reports back with its review complete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-493r:
Numbers on Hispanic staff across the federal workforce fill GAO-07-493R, released May 18, 2007. The volume builds on an August 2006 GAO report that Congress requested. That study asked what shapes Hispanic hiring and promotion in federal jobs. It also covered the roles of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the Office of Personnel Management. Both bodies require agencies to scan their own workforces for barriers.

This data report breaks the figures down in finer cuts. It shows Hispanic shares by agency, by job type, and by grade level. New hires get their own cut. Each figure sits next to the Hispanic share of the civilian labor force. The scope is the executive branch minus intelligence agencies, the Postal Service, and the Foreign Service. GAO offers the tables as a base for deeper study, not as a verdict on any one agency.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-503r:
Iraqi forces can fight better than they can supply themselves, and GAO-07-503R, dated March 28, 2007, reports early proof. The letter covers the support side of two ministries, Defense and Interior. It asks how well each one handles logistics, command and control, and intelligence. GAO also picked up facts on how the two ministries talk to each other.

The work began on the Comptroller General's own call, given broad interest in Congress. A classified version went to Congress on March 7, 2007. This text is the open version, with secret details stripped out. GAO briefed a House panel on March 9, 2007 about army and police logistics. A deeper follow-up was promised. It will weigh U.S. support levels and how Iraqi self-reliance links to U.S. troop drawdown. Early signs showed supply chains lagging far behind combat growth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-533r:
Written answers after a Senate hearing fill GAO-07-533R, a GAO letter dated February 27, 2007. On December 5, 2006, GAO testified on the Improper Payments Information Act of 2002. That law forces agencies to find and report payments made in error. At the hearing's close, senators asked for more in writing. This letter is the reply.

Three questions shape the answers. The first asks what blocks agencies from cutting bad payments. The second asks which law changes would clear those blocks. The third seeks draft words to amend the act itself. GAO's draft aims at fuller disclosure of error rates and cleanup plans. The letter is short and pointed. It turns hearing talk into text that staff can drop into a bill, which is its whole purpose.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-593r:
Banking questions from Congress get a briefing in letter form in GAO-07-593R, dated April 30, 2007. The letter gathers facts on federal actions that shape the banking trade. Topics run from the savings and loan crisis to trade finance and tax policy. Bank profits and executive pay also feature. One topic, bank fees, was split off for a later report by agreement with staff.

GAO first briefed the staff on December 11, 2006, from early work. This letter writes that brief down and brings it current. It is a fact pack, not an audit with a verdict. Readers get the history and the numbers behind each policy strand. The letter shows how past crises still steer today's rules. It also flags where pay at the top of big banks has run ahead of the industry's own story. Congress ordered the pack as groundwork for oversight hearings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-623r:
Small scissors came back to airplane cabins, and GAO-07-623R, dated April 25, 2007, checks what followed. In December 2005, the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) eased its banned items list. Travelers may again carry metal scissors with blades of 4 inches or less. Small tools of 7 inches or less, minus a few types, also pass. The alleged August 2006 liquid bomb plot kept the stakes high.

A spending law's conference report told GAO to study the change. GAO asked what facts drove the choice and what airlines, crews, and screeners think of it. It then hunted for harm: no security incident tied to the freed items had been reported. Effects on checkpoint flow were murkier, since lines shift for many reasons. The letter lays out the basis and the open ends, so Congress can judge the risk call itself.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-663r:
One charter group in the April batch failed its audit duty, and GAO-07-663R, a GAO letter of April 5, 2007, says so plainly. The American GI Forum of the United States is a federally chartered corporation. Its purposes include upholding the Constitution and the flag and fostering the principles of American democracy. Under 36 U.S.C. 10101, such bodies must file yearly financial statements and obtain an audit by an outside public accountant.

For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2005, the forum did not obtain that audit. Officials told GAO the statements had been reviewed instead, which does not meet the law. They said a full audit is planned in the future. GAO thus found a reportable breach of the reporting rules, unlike the clean results in its peer letters that month. The letter is short because the fact is short: a required audit was skipped.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-773r:
How the Federal Aviation Administration pays for air traffic control is weighed in GAO-07-773R, a letter dated June 8, 2007. In February 2007, the White House proposed user fees for the agency. Commercial users would pay charges tied to the cost of service. Many current aviation taxes would end. Fuel taxes for private flyers would rise sharply. The plan rested on a cost study the agency released in January 2007. GAO compared the plan with practices in other nations.

Other countries fund air traffic control through direct user charges. Their methods split costs among airlines, cargo firms, and private flyers in varied ways. GAO set the U.S. proposal beside those models. It showed where the cost study's choices match or differ from practice abroad. The letter aims to help Congress judge the fee plan. The agency's funding law expired at the end of fiscal year 2007.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-783r:
War spending totals are reported in GAO-07-783R, a letter GAO sent on May 18, 2007. Since 2001, Congress has given the Defense Department hundreds of billions for the Global War on Terrorism. Reported war costs rose from about $0.2 billion in fiscal year 2001. They hit about $98.4 billion in fiscal year 2006. For fiscal year 2007, Congress had given $70 billion so far. The department sought $93.4 billion more that year. It asked for $141.7 billion for fiscal year 2008.

The department compiles war costs in a monthly execution report. Leaders use it to advise Congress and shape budget requests. Future costs hinge on the pace and length of operations. Bases abroad, troop moves, and gear repair also drive the totals. GAO's letter passes on the department's reported obligations. It frames the choices leaders face as costs climb. Long-term fiscal strain makes those trade-offs harder each year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-803r:
A plan to move warning missions out of Cheyenne Mountain is reviewed in GAO-07-803R, a letter dated May 21, 2007. The Colorado site was built in the early 1960s to survive a nuclear strike. Its teams watch for air, missile, and space threats to North America. Upgrades to its warning systems cost over $700 million from fiscal years 2000 to 2006. In July 2006, commanders announced a shift of some work to Peterson Air Force Base. They projected savings of $150 million to $200 million a year.

GAO found the full costs of the move had not been pinned down. The security effects of leaving the hardened site were also unclear. Missile warning work was also set to move to Schriever Air Force Base. Leaders said the missile strike threat no longer justifies the mountain site. GAO's letter weighs what the plan would truly save. It tests whether split operations raise risks for the warning mission.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-893r:
The 2006 evacuation of Americans from Lebanon is reviewed in GAO-07-893R, a letter dated June 7, 2007. Nearly 15,000 citizens left during July and August 2006. It was one of the largest such evacuations in recent history. The State Department leads evacuations abroad. The Defense Department supplied ships, aircraft, and security in a war zone. GAO briefed congressional staff on April 30, 2007. This letter transmits that briefing.

Embassies keep emergency action plans and count Americans in their countries. The two departments hold an agreement that sets their roles. War erupted suddenly after a July 12 kidnapping of Israeli soldiers. Israel bombed Beirut's airport and blockaded the ports. Planning began July 14, and small groups left by helicopter on July 16. The first large boat group sailed July 19 for Cyprus. GAO weighed the operation's successes and strains. Speed and coordination under fire stand out.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-983r:
The long-term federal budget path is updated in GAO-07-983R, a letter dated June 4, 2007. Since 1992, GAO has run simulations of deficits and debt. Members of Congress from both parties asked for the model. This update uses fresh Social Security and Medicare estimates. The alternative path now assumes more realistic Medicare growth. Revenues return to their historical share in that path. The bottom line stays grim under both paths. Current fiscal policy cannot hold over the long run.

Debt climbs to levels that crowd out other choices. Health costs drive most of the pressure ahead. The letter refreshes numbers three times a year by design. Trustee reports and budget outlooks feed the model. No new policy advice comes with the figures. The update exists to keep the warning current. Lawmakers get the trend lines in plain form. Delay raises the cost of every fix.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1003r:
Answers to follow-up questions from a hearing on disaster readiness form GAO letter GAO-08-1003R, dated July 15, 2008. Committee members sent the questions after GAO testified on the Department of Homeland Security's readiness for catastrophic disasters. The hearing was held by a House subcommittee on management and oversight.

The answers rest on GAO work already issued, done under standard audit rules. They add detail on how the department prepares for events that could overwhelm normal response. Because the material draws on prior work, GAO did not seek fresh comments from the department. The letter stands as the formal record of those replies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-143r:
Iraqi security forces and their support systems are assessed in GAO letter GAO-08-143R of November 30, 2007. Coalition training has raised Iraqi troop and police numbers from over 171,000 in July 2005 to about 359,600 in September 2007. Iraqi commands now run most army divisions and the national police. Yet the forces lean on coalition help behind the lines.

Logistics, command and control, and intelligence skills remain half-built. Violence, sectarian strife, and weak ministries slow their growth. GAO warned that claims of independent units ring unclear while support lags. It urged the Defense Department to define its readiness terms and show how it grades units.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-173r:
Weaknesses at a nuclear weapons lab are cataloged in GAO letter GAO-08-173R of January 10, 2008. Los Alamos National Laboratory designs nuclear weapons for the nation's stockpile. Over a decade, GAO has logged flaws in its security, safety, and project work. In July 2004, the lab halted operations after classified computer disks were lost. The review found more than 3,400 security and safety issues.

A new firm took over the lab in June 2006 after open competition. The letter briefs Congress on four fronts. They are the guarding of classified data, controls on nuclear material, worker and nuclear safety, and project management.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-203r:
Airport tax receipts are traced in GAO letter GAO-08-203R, dated November 2, 2007. The Airport and Airway Trust Fund draws excise taxes tied to air travel. The transport department asked GAO to test whether the sums sent to the fund for fiscal year 2007 rest on sound records. The department agreed to the procedures in advance.

The agreed checks reached from raw transactions up to final transfers. Quarterly certifications from the tax agency came under review. So did adjustments booked by the Treasury's payment service during the year. GAO further probed how the tax analysis office estimates receipts before final counts land. As with its highway twin, the letter makes no claim that the chosen checks were the right ones.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-373r:
Defense critical infrastructure risk analysis is reviewed in GAO letter GAO-08-373R, dated April 2, 2008. The Defense Critical Infrastructure Program, set up in August 2005, lists assets the Defense Department needs to carry out its missions. Each listed asset must get a vulnerability assessment.

GAO found that the program's asset lists leave out highly sensitive sites tied to Sensitive Compartmented Information and Special Access Programs. The Joint Staff asked only for assets classified at the collateral level, so some groups held back their most sensitive items. The Defense Intelligence Agency alone had not sent in over 80 assets it judged critical. GAO warned that the gaps leave the risk picture incomplete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-423r:
Reported Defense Department obligations for the Global War on Terrorism are tallied in GAO letter GAO-08-423R, dated January 30, 2008. Congress has given the department hundreds of billions of dollars for these operations since 2001. The letter tracks the reported figures year by year.

Reported obligations climbed from about $0.2 billion in fiscal year 2001 to about $139.8 billion in fiscal year 2007. For fiscal year 2007, Congress provided about $161.8 billion in yearly and supplemental funds. For fiscal year 2008, Congress had provided about $86.8 billion as of December 2007, including $16.8 billion for Mine Resistant Ambush Protected vehicles. The department reported $23.8 billion in obligations for fiscal year 2008 through November 2007. The letter frames the trade-offs these sums force on a tight long-term budget.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-663r:
Rust eats ships, planes, and trucks, and the Defense Department spends to slow it. GAO-08-663R, a letter dated April 15, 2008, reviews the department's fiscal year 2009 budget request for corrosion prevention and control. Law required the review within 60 days of the budget filing.

The request holds about $14.1 million for the corrosion program office. About $10.7 million would fund projects, and $3.4 million would fund other corrosion work. Project picks were due in summer 2008. GAO compared the request with stated needs and the payoff the work could bring. One limit: the department's own corrosion report had not yet arrived.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-753r:
A test power let the Defense Department judge bids for computer services on best value, not just low price. The power, set in a fiscal year 2004 law, was due to end on September 30, 2008. GAO-08-753R, a letter dated May 29, 2008, reports whether the test was ever tried.

No part of the department ever asked to use the power. With no trials, GAO cannot judge if the approach is fair or works well. The Army, Navy, and Air Force see no need to extend it. One agency, the Defense Logistics Agency, backs an extension. Top officials made no request to Congress either way.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-783r:
Federal debt paths point up for decades under current trends. GAO-08-783R, a letter dated May 16, 2008, updates the long-term fiscal outlook GAO has charted since 1992. The update runs two paths to 2050: one holds current law, and one keeps recent policy habits.

Both paths show the outlook is not sustainable. Health costs, more than any other force, drive the gap. Nearly 80 million Americans will claim Social Security over the next two decades, an average of more than 10,000 a day. The oldest boomers can claim Medicare in less than 3 years. The letter frames the scale of the fix ahead.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-853r:
War spending counts keep climbing in GAO-08-853R, a letter dated June 13, 2008. It reports what the Defense Department says it has obligated for the Global War on Terrorism. Yearly sums rose from about $0.2 billion in fiscal year 2001 to about $139.8 billion in fiscal year 2007.

For fiscal year 2008 the President asked for $189.3 billion. By May 2008 Congress had given about $86.8 billion of that, including $16.8 billion for blast-proof trucks. A further $102.5 billion awaited action. The fiscal year 2009 ask adds about $66 billion. The letter frames the trade-offs these sums force on the budget.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-863r:
Bank insurance funds rest on careful bookkeeping at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. GAO-08-863R, a management report dated July 11, 2008, lists control flaws found during the audit of the calendar year 2007 statements for two funds the agency runs.

Checks sent to a Dallas mailroom were not booked properly. Guards for checks in transit were thin, raising theft and loss risk. Payment approvals in the accounting system did not always catch errors in time, so costs could land in the wrong bucket. None of the flaws counted as grave. Five fixes are proposed, and the agency agreed with them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-893r:
Royalty cash from oil and gas on federal lands topped $9 billion in fiscal year 2007. The Minerals Management Service collects it, sending more than $5 billion to the Treasury. GAO-08-893R, a letter dated September 12, 2008, warns that weak data habits put that income at risk.

Firms report their own output and royalty sums each month. Inspectors check meters and records on more than 28,000 active leases, but findings live in clashing databases. Drilling permit requests rose from about 4,000 in 2001 to more than 10,000 in 2007, stretching the checks. Oil prices above $140 a barrel raise the cost of any missed gallon.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-933r:
Bomb-sniffing dog teams at airports and transit systems are the subject of GAO-08-933R, a July 2008 letter that formally sends Congress a briefing. The Transportation Security Administration runs a national program that buys, trains, deploys, and certifies the teams, each a dog paired with a handler. A 2007 law told the homeland security secretary to add up to 200 certified teams a year through the end of 2010 and told GAO to report on the program.

The briefing asks three things. Does TSA have a plan to meet the mandated growth? Does it have the capacity to train and field that many teams? And is it on track so far? It also covers dog programs run by other homeland security components, so lawmakers see the full picture in one place.
